title: The induction step in relative dimension one
statement: Let $f:X\to S$ be an affine morphism [pqf-def-affine-morphism] which is smooth of relative dimension one [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms], with $X$ affine. Let $n\geq1$ be an integer invertible on $S$, and let $q\geq1$ be an integer. Assume that $\mathrm{BC}(f,n,q')$ holds universally for every $0\leq q'\leq q-1$, in the sense of [sbc-def-base-change-property]. Then $\mathrm{BC}(f,n,q)$ holds universally, and hence $\mathrm{BC}(f,n,q')$ holds universally for every $0\leq q'\leq q$.

proof.text: Suppose $\mathrm{BC}(f,n,q)$ fails universally. The hypothesis supplies the universal cumulative lower-degree assumption of [sbc-lem-bc-universal-test], and $q\geq1$: its phrase "all $q'\leq q-1$" ranges over the nonnegative degrees on which [sbc-def-base-change-property] defines $\mathrm{BC}$. That lemma gives two Cartesian squares $X\leftarrow X'\leftarrow Y$ above $S\leftarrow S'\leftarrow\operatorname{Spec}K$, with $f':X'\to S'$ a base change of $f$, $S'$ affine, integral and normal with algebraically closed function field $L$, $K$ algebraically closed, $\operatorname{Spec}K\to S'$ dominant, and an integer $d\mid n$ with $R^qh_*(\mathbf Z/d\mathbf Z)\ne0$ for the horizontal map $h:Y\to X'$, while $e:Y\to\operatorname{Spec}K$ is the vertical map in the corrected diagram of the cited statement. Write $S'=\operatorname{Spec}A$. Dominance means that $A\to K$ is injective: its kernel is the prime giving the image point, which is the generic point $(0)$ of the integral scheme $S'$. Thus it extends to the inclusion $L=\operatorname{Frac}A\to K$, and the bottom arrow is the composite $\operatorname{Spec}K\to\operatorname{Spec}L\to\operatorname{Spec}A$. In the stated Lean interface, the embedding i from the function field into K and the factorization of the bottom map are already part of the failure witness, so no separate extension construction is necessary.

proof.text: By clause (1) of [lem-weil-pbc-affine-morphism-permanence], $f'$ is affine; since $S'$ is affine, clause (2) makes $X'$ affine. By clause (1) of [lem-sbc-smooth-relative-dimension-permanence], $f'$ is smooth of relative dimension one. These are statements about arbitrary base changes, so they apply to the first Cartesian square produced in step 1. In particular no affineness of the original base $S$ is being assumed.

source.place: Tag 0EYU, theorem-smooth-base-change, second proof: reduction by lemma-base-change-does-not-hold (Tag 0F08) and final curve-test argument

proof.text: The integer $n$ is invertible on $S'$: pull back its inverse on $S$ along $S'\to S$ (as also specified in [sbc-def-base-change-property]). Write $n=da$ with $a\in\mathbf Z$. At every stalk of $\mathcal O_{S'}$, if $v$ is the inverse of $n$, then $d(av)=(da)v=nv=1$. Consequently $d$ is invertible on $S'$. This argument also covers negative $d$; because $n\geq1$ and $d\mid n$, $d$ is nonzero.

source.place: Tag 0EYU, theorem-smooth-base-change, second proof: reduction by lemma-base-change-does-not-hold (Tag 0F08) and final curve-test argument

proof.text: Apply [sbc-thm-universal-test-vanishing] to the second Cartesian square, with $X'$ in place of $X$, $S'$ in place of $S$, the inclusions $A\subset L\subset K$ of step 1, and the integer $d$. Step 1 supplies normality, the algebraically closed function field and extension; step 2 supplies affine smooth relative dimension one and the affine source; step 3 supplies invertibility of $d$. As $q\geq1$, the theorem gives $R^qh_*(\mathbf Z/d\mathbf Z)=0$, contradicting its nonvanishing in step 1. To apply the ring-based Lean theorem, set A = Γ(S′, O) and L = S′.functionField. Mathlib identifies L as the fraction field of A. Transport the normal stalks across S′ ≅ Spec A using the stalk ring isomorphisms, and postcompose the square by this base isomorphism. The identity fromSpecStalk_toSpecΓ identifies the bottom arrow with the two Spec maps of the algebra maps A → L → K. Apply the vanishing theorem with the integer cast of the natural divisor d; its absolute value is d, and rightDerivedLowerStarPlus unfolds to the derived pushforward in the failure witness.

source.place: Tag 0EYU, theorem-smooth-base-change, second proof: reduction by lemma-base-change-does-not-hold (Tag 0F08) and final curve-test argument

proof.text: The supposition in step 1 is therefore impossible, so $\mathrm{BC}(f,n,q)$ holds universally. For any $0\leq q'\leq q$, either $q'=q$, when this conclusion applies, or $q'<q$, when integrality gives $q'\leq q-1$ and the original hypothesis applies. By [sbc-def-base-change-property] this is precisely $\mathrm{UBC}^{\leq q}(f,n)$. There is no need to repeat the contradiction on a second base: step 1 already detected failure of the universal property.
